proposals.label: AI as epochal transformation
proposals.definition: AI described as a defining, epochal transformation of the era or of society, often within the broader digital/ICT revolution, including reflections on the nature of intelligence or on AI and human values.
proposals.inclusion: Passages calling AI a revolution comparable to steam or electricity, the defining test of the age, a force transforming how people live, or philosophical reflection on AI.
proposals.exclusion: Brief listing among technologies (AI_TECH_LIST_MENTION); specific economic effects (AI_ECONOMY_LABOR).
proposals.boundary_cases: Pandemic-accelerated digitalisation that names AI is coded here when AI's transformative role is described rather than just listed.

examples.quote: Steam powered the industrial revolution. The transistor powered the digital age. No force in our time is as profound as artificial intelligence.

proposals.label: AI listed among technologies
proposals.definition: AI named only briefly in a neutral or positive list of technologies, trends or national strengths, without further discussion of AI itself.
proposals.inclusion: Passages where 'artificial intelligence' appears alongside other technologies (robotics, big data, quantum, biotech) with no AI-specific claim.
proposals.exclusion: AI listed among threats or crises (AI_THREAT_LIST_MENTION); any passage with an AI-specific claim (use the substantive code).
proposals.boundary_cases: A list plus one AI-specific sentence should receive the substantive code instead of, or in addition to, this code.

examples.quote: We are convinced that globalization, information technology, artificial intelligence and real-time communication are tools

proposals.label: AI listed among threats or crises
proposals.definition: AI named briefly within a catalogue of global challenges, threats or citizen worries (conflict, climate, pandemics, disinformation, cost of living) without elaboration of the AI risk itself.
proposals.inclusion: Passages where AI or 'unregulated AI' is one item in a list of crises, dangers or public concerns, or noted as neglected on a crowded agenda.
proposals.exclusion: Passages that explain how AI causes the harm (use the specific risk code); neutral technology lists (AI_TECH_LIST_MENTION).
proposals.boundary_cases: If the passage says AI is a threat and names a mechanism (e.g. weapons, disinformation), use that mechanism's code.

examples.quote: risks of cyberwarfare and the inappropriate application of artificial intelligence

proposals.label: International AI rules and governance
proposals.definition: Calls for, or discussion of, international rules, norms, legal frameworks, standards, treaties or cooperative mechanisms to govern AI, including arguments that governance must keep pace with AI and must balance innovation with protection.
proposals.inclusion: Passages urging common/binding/global rules, regulation, guardrails, norms, principles or multilateral cooperation on AI; references to non-UN governance initiatives (G7 Hiroshima Process, G20, AI safety summits, GPAI) as governance.
proposals.exclusion: Purely national regulation (AI_NATIONAL_STRATEGY); UN-specific bodies and processes (AI_UN_ROLE); demands centred on developing countries' voice in rule-making (AI_INCLUSIVE_GOVERNANCE); rejection of international governance (AI_GOVERNANCE_SKEPTICISM); weapons-specific rules (AI_MILITARY_WEAPONS).
proposals.boundary_cases: A passage calling for global rules through the UN can take both AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE and AI_UN_ROLE. Generic 'responsible AI' wording without any governance mechanism or call for rules is coded here only if it addresses how AI should be governed collectively.

examples.quote: The governance of new spheres of human activity, including artificial intelligence, the Internet and outer space, must keep up with the speed and scale

proposals.label: Equal voice in AI rule-making
proposals.definition: Demands that developing, African, small or all states have a meaningful, equal say in setting AI rules and standards, and objections to AI rules being written by a few states or in exclusive formats outside the UN.
proposals.inclusion: Passages insisting that the Global South, Africa, small states or every country participate in shaping AI governance; criticism that AI rules are made by narrow clubs or favour some nations.
proposals.exclusion: Unequal access to AI technology or benefits without a rule-making claim (AI_DIGITAL_DIVIDE); general calls for 'inclusive' governance with no claim about who sets the rules (AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE).
proposals.boundary_cases: When a passage links mineral supply or market size to a demand for a seat at the AI rule-making table, code here (and AI_RESOURCE_FOOTPRINT only if resource demand is discussed).

examples.quote: in circumvention of the United Nations — to create subordinate, narrow formats to resolve crucial issues, such as control over the Internet or determination of legal frameworks to use artificial intelligence technologies

proposals.label: UN bodies and processes on AI
proposals.definition: References to the UN system's role on AI: the Secretary-General's advisory body, Tech Envoy, Global Digital Compact, Pact for the Future, Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, Global Dialogue on AI Governance, GA/Security Council agenda items, UNESCO initiatives, or the UN using AI for its own work.
proposals.inclusion: Passages supporting, criticising, leading or proposing UN AI bodies, resolutions, processes or agenda items; the UN as the central forum for AI decisions; AI to make the UN more efficient.
proposals.exclusion: International governance calls that do not mention the UN system or its instruments (AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE).
proposals.boundary_cases: Criticism that the UN lags or is bypassed counts here when it calls for a UN role; outright rejection of a UN role is AI_GOVERNANCE_SKEPTICISM.

examples.quote: the welcome role that the United Nations is trying to play in confronting emerging challenges, such as digital cooperation, crime, cybersecurity and artificial intelligence

proposals.label: Military AI and autonomous weapons
proposals.definition: AI in warfare, weapons and strategic security: lethal autonomous weapons systems, military targeting, AI in nuclear command and escalation, and calls for rules, bans or human control over military AI.
proposals.inclusion: Passages on autonomous weapons, machines deciding life and death, AI on the battlefield, military AI norms or treaties, AI as a strategic/arms-control risk alongside nuclear, cyber and space.
proposals.exclusion: Non-military AI safety or loss-of-control risks (AI_SAFETY_EXISTENTIAL); criminal or terrorist misuse and cyberattacks (AI_CYBER_SECURITY); AI used to support arms-control verification or peace (AI_PEACE_APPLICATIONS).
proposals.boundary_cases: Human control of weapons is coded here, not AI_HUMAN_CONTROL. A list of threats merely naming 'AI' next to war is AI_THREAT_LIST_MENTION unless military use of AI is stated.

examples.quote: We are already seeing the impacts on civilians as armed forces increasingly integrate AI capabilities into their targeting systems in warfare.

proposals.label: AI as a tool for peace
proposals.definition: AI presented as a tool for diplomacy, mediation, conflict prevention, arms-control verification or as a force that should serve peace rather than domination.
proposals.inclusion: Passages proposing AI for early warning of conflict, mediation, translation for diplomacy, treaty verification, or insisting AI serve peace not domination.
proposals.exclusion: AI for development, health or climate (AI_DEVELOPMENT_SDGS); military AI risks (AI_MILITARY_WEAPONS).
proposals.boundary_cases: Disaster early warning is development/climate (AI_DEVELOPMENT_SDGS), not peace, unless conflict prevention is stated.

examples.quote: the artificial intelligence technologies as force for peace, not tools for domination

proposals.label: Frontier AI safety and loss of control
proposals.definition: Technical and catastrophic AI risks: frontier model safety, misalignment, superintelligence, loss of control, uncontrolled or ungoverned AI as a survival or existential threat, and safety testing before release.
proposals.inclusion: Passages warning of AI escaping human control, existential or species-level risk, superintelligence, safety requirements for the most capable models.
proposals.exclusion: Military uses (AI_MILITARY_WEAPONS); general normative insistence that humans stay in charge without a safety-risk claim (AI_HUMAN_CONTROL); disinformation or crime (their own codes).
proposals.boundary_cases: A brief 'uncontrolled use of AI' warning with no catastrophic or technical safety content goes to AI_OPPORTUNITY_RISK_DUALITY or AI_THREAT_LIST_MENTION.

examples.quote: we are on a precipice either of a technology-fueled utopia or an apocalypse

proposals.label: Human agency, control and accountability
proposals.definition: Normative insistence that humans remain in control of AI and responsible for AI-assisted decisions, that people stay subjects rather than objects of algorithms, and that human judgment, autonomy and legal accountability be preserved.
proposals.inclusion: Passages saying technology must remain under human control, humans must be masters of AI, decisions must stay with accountable people, or warning against outsourcing human thought and free will to machines.
proposals.exclusion: Human control of weapons (AI_MILITARY_WEAPONS); catastrophic loss-of-control risk (AI_SAFETY_EXISTENTIAL); broad human rights and ethics language without the control/agency claim (AI_HUMAN_RIGHTS_ETHICS).
proposals.boundary_cases: 'Human-centred AI' alone is AI_HUMAN_RIGHTS_ETHICS; it is coded here only when human control, decision authority or accountability is explicit.

examples.quote: We call for ethical, responsible, inclusive, and human-centered development and use of artificial intelligence with appropriate safeguard

proposals.label: Human rights, ethics and democracy
proposals.definition: AI framed through human rights, dignity, ethics, privacy, surveillance, human-centred design and democratic values, including risks of repression, algorithmic control of citizens and erosion of democratic accountability.
proposals.inclusion: Passages calling for human-centred, rights-based or ethical AI, protection of privacy and freedoms, warning of AI surveillance or repression, or tying AI to democracy and accountability.
proposals.exclusion: Discrimination, stereotypes and cultural/linguistic exclusion (AI_BIAS_CULTURAL_DIVERSITY); children specifically (AI_CHILD_PROTECTION); disinformation (AI_DISINFORMATION).
proposals.boundary_cases: Ethics invoked as part of a call for international rules takes both this code and AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE.

examples.quote: AI tools have to be made for humanity, lest we become the source material for AI systems to use

proposals.label: Bias, stereotypes and cultural diversity
proposals.definition: AI reproducing bias, prejudice, hate or stereotypes, distorting or censoring history, misrepresenting peoples, and threatening or protecting linguistic and cultural diversity.
proposals.inclusion: Passages on biased training data, discrimination, AI spreading hatred or stereotypes, digital erasure of non-hegemonic cultures, fair representation in AI-mediated knowledge, preserving small languages or multilingualism.
proposals.exclusion: General human rights or ethics language without bias or cultural content (AI_HUMAN_RIGHTS_ETHICS); disinformation campaigns (AI_DISINFORMATION).
proposals.boundary_cases: AI used to protect small languages (a positive application) is coded here because the concern is cultural diversity.

examples.quote: Misuse of AI is sharpening bias and diluting mutual respect.

proposals.label: Disinformation and information integrity
proposals.definition: AI-enabled misinformation, disinformation, deepfakes, manipulation of public opinion, election interference and threats to information integrity.
proposals.inclusion: Passages linking AI to fake content, deepfakes, propaganda, manipulated elections or the erosion of shared facts.
proposals.exclusion: Hate speech and stereotypes without a falsehood claim (AI_BIAS_CULTURAL_DIVERSITY); cybercrime (AI_CYBER_SECURITY).
proposals.boundary_cases: A list naming 'artificial intelligence' and 'disinformation' as separate items does not link them; code AI_THREAT_LIST_MENTION unless the text connects AI to disinformation.

examples.quote: Many young people have fallen victim to those negative practices.

proposals.label: Cyber threats, crime and terrorist misuse
proposals.definition: AI misuse by criminals, terrorists or hostile actors: cyberattacks, cybercrime, attacks on critical infrastructure, online crime, and AI within international information-security frameworks.
proposals.inclusion: Passages on AI-enabled cyberattacks, fraud, trafficking, terrorism or hybrid threats, and on cybercrime cooperation covering AI.
proposals.exclusion: State military use of AI in warfare (AI_MILITARY_WEAPONS); disinformation (AI_DISINFORMATION).
proposals.boundary_cases: Passages that discuss only cyberspace or new technologies without naming AI are not AI evidence.

examples.quote: increasingly being used for incitement, terrorist recruitment and spreading hate speech, misinformation and disinformation, with adverse effects on cybersecurity

proposals.label: AI divide and equitable access
proposals.definition: Inequality in access to AI and its benefits between and within countries: risks of a new AI divide, North-South gaps, developing countries as passive consumers, and calls to share AI benefits with all.
proposals.inclusion: Passages warning AI will widen gaps or leave countries behind, demanding equitable access or benefit-sharing, or envisioning AI for all.
proposals.exclusion: Concrete support measures such as training, funding or technology transfer (AI_CAPACITY_BUILDING); rule-making voice (AI_INCLUSIVE_GOVERNANCE); concentration of power in firms or states (AI_SOVEREIGNTY_CONCENTRATION).
proposals.boundary_cases: When a passage states both the divide and a remedy (e.g. capacity building), apply both codes.

examples.quote: it is becoming imperative for all countries to have access to the Internet, including artificial intelligence, which is revolutionizing the world as we speak

proposals.label: Capacity building and AI cooperation
proposals.definition: Concrete cooperation to build AI capabilities: skills, training, technology transfer, financing, infrastructure, regional AI centres and bilateral or South-South AI partnerships.
proposals.inclusion: Passages offering or requesting AI training, funds, compute, infrastructure, knowledge sharing, regional centres or partnerships.
proposals.exclusion: Statements of inequality without a support measure (AI_DIGITAL_DIVIDE); a country's own domestic programmes (AI_NATIONAL_STRATEGY).
proposals.boundary_cases: A country offering its national AI experience to others takes this code and AI_NATIONAL_STRATEGY.

examples.quote: including Leadership and Governance in the Age of Digital Technologies and Artificial Intelligence

proposals.label: AI for development and the SDGs
proposals.definition: AI as a means to advance sustainable development, growth, health, agriculture, education systems, public services, climate action and disaster early warning, including particular value for small and island states.
proposals.inclusion: Passages presenting AI as a tool for the SDGs, poverty reduction, health, food security, climate mitigation or adaptation, disaster prediction or better services.
proposals.exclusion: Jobs and labour-market effects (AI_ECONOMY_LABOR); environmental costs of AI (AI_RESOURCE_FOOTPRINT); a country describing its own AI investments (AI_NATIONAL_STRATEGY).
proposals.boundary_cases: If AI is only listed among technologies that could help development without elaboration, prefer AI_TECH_LIST_MENTION.

examples.quote: international attention and investments should be directed towards those technologies in order to accelerate sustainable development

proposals.label: Energy, minerals and environmental footprint
proposals.definition: Material demands of AI: energy and water consumption, data-centre footprints, and rising demand for critical minerals, including producer countries' claims about value addition.
proposals.inclusion: Passages linking AI to energy demand, water or land use, emissions of AI infrastructure, or critical-mineral supply.
proposals.exclusion: AI used to fight climate change (AI_DEVELOPMENT_SDGS); chip supply-chain rivalry (AI_GEOPOLITICAL_RIVALRY).
proposals.boundary_cases: Minerals raised mainly to claim a rule-making seat also take AI_INCLUSIVE_GOVERNANCE.

examples.quote: managing the enormous demands that tech infrastructure places on water, energy, land, and other resources

proposals.label: Youth, education and skills
proposals.definition: AI in relation to young people, schools and education: preparing youth for AI, AI literacy, AI in teaching, and disruptions such as plagiarism.
proposals.inclusion: Passages about equipping youth with AI skills, AI's effect on learning or schools, or generative AI disrupting education.
proposals.exclusion: Child online safety and exploitation (AI_CHILD_PROTECTION); international capacity-building programmes (AI_CAPACITY_BUILDING).
proposals.boundary_cases: Youth employment effects of AI can take this code and AI_ECONOMY_LABOR.

examples.quote: We have a youthful population ready to play a key role in the beneficiation at source of critical minerals and research and innovations for artificial intelligence.

proposals.label: National AI strategy and achievements
proposals.definition: A speaker's own country's AI strategies, investments, programmes, regulation, pilots, institutions, talent and leadership claims, including domestic regulatory approaches such as sandboxes.
proposals.inclusion: Passages describing national AI plans, investments, data centres, public-service pilots, national AI laws or sandboxes, or claims of national AI leadership or hosting AI events and centres.
proposals.exclusion: International cooperation offered to others (AI_CAPACITY_BUILDING); calls for international rules (AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE).
proposals.boundary_cases: Hosting a UN/UNESCO AI centre takes this code and AI_UN_ROLE.

examples.quote: My country focuses on anticipating challenges and on investing in advanced fields, such as artificial intelligence, space technology and renewable energy.

proposals.label: Power concentration, dependence and sovereignty
proposals.definition: Concern that AI power, data, compute and wealth are concentrated in a few companies or countries, creating dependence, domination or new hierarchies, and claims to digital sovereignty, national AI models or public rather than oligarchic control.
proposals.inclusion: Passages about big tech or tech oligarchs, monopolies, distrust of corporate self-regulation, technological dependence, AI as a tool of domination or neo-colonialism, and sovereign AI capacity.
proposals.exclusion: Access gaps without a power/control claim (AI_DIGITAL_DIVIDE); strategic competition between great powers (AI_GEOPOLITICAL_RIVALRY); rule-making exclusion (AI_INCLUSIVE_GOVERNANCE).
proposals.boundary_cases: Anti-capitalist framing of AI as a systemic threat is coded here when it centres on concentrated control or wealth.

examples.quote: Technological progress must not become a new instrument of domination. Africa must also be a center of creativity, innovation, and digital sovereignty.

proposals.label: AI as both promise and peril
proposals.definition: Explicit framing of AI as double-edged: great opportunity alongside serious risk, a neutral tool whose effects depend on use, or public fears to be answered with reassurance.
proposals.inclusion: Passages that pair AI's benefits with its dangers, call it a double-edged sword, or state that its impact depends on human choices.
proposals.exclusion: Passages that discuss only a specific risk or only a benefit (use the specific code).
proposals.boundary_cases: Duality language that leads directly into a governance call takes both this code and AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE.

examples.quote: What is know called the fourth industrial revolution presents both a challenge and an opportunity.

proposals.label: AI listed among technologies
proposals.definition: AI named only briefly in a neutral or positive list of technologies, trends or national strengths, without further discussion of AI itself.
proposals.inclusion: Passages where 'artificial intelligence' appears alongside other technologies (robotics, big data, quantum, biotech) with no AI-specific claim.
proposals.exclusion: AI listed among threats or crises (AI_THREAT_LIST_MENTION); any passage with an AI-specific claim (use the substantive code).
proposals.boundary_cases: A list plus one AI-specific sentence should receive the substantive code instead of, or in addition to, this code.

examples.quote: joining the revolutions currently taking place in the fields of artificial intelligence, digitalization and renewable energy

proposals.label: AI listed among threats or crises
proposals.definition: AI named briefly within a catalogue of global challenges, threats or citizen worries (conflict, climate, pandemics, disinformation, cost of living) without elaboration of the AI risk itself.
proposals.inclusion: Passages where AI or 'unregulated AI' is one item in a list of crises, dangers or public concerns, or noted as neglected on a crowded agenda.
proposals.exclusion: Passages that explain how AI causes the harm (use the specific risk code); neutral technology lists (AI_TECH_LIST_MENTION).
proposals.boundary_cases: If the passage says AI is a threat and names a mechanism (e.g. weapons, disinformation), use that mechanism's code.

examples.quote: They are also concerned about artificial intelligence, foreign interference, misinformation and disinformation.

examples.text: My country is also playing a vital role in promoting humanitarian and relief assistance to areas affected by conflicts and disasters around the world. The United Arab Emirates aspires to transform the whole region into a global centre for technology, culture and innovation after decades of crises. My country focuses on anticipating challenges and on investing in advanced fields, such as artificial intelligence, space technology and renewable energy. I would like to emphasize that empowering women and youth and investing in their unlimited skills contribute to building resilient and cohesive societies and, eventually, stable and safe countries.

Secondly, new issues are emerging that demand multilateral solutions in accordance with normative and cooperative arrangements. What is know called the fourth industrial revolution presents both a challenge and an opportunity. From artificial intelligence and robotization to the implementation of smart grids and 5G infrastructure and data management, to restructuring entire sectors of the economy, the impact of new technologies — on the economy, the work world and relations among States — will demand new rules of conduct at the international level. The UN must play a central role in defining them by providing compromise solutions capable of safeguard the public interest.

I can assure everyone that, like many people in the countries of our Organization, Canadians, too, are worried about the cost of living. They are also concerned about artificial intelligence, foreign interference, misinformation and disinformation.

We come once again to the Assembly with a positive and optimistic vision of humankind, but we must not be naive. Objectively, we live in a better world, although of course our current reality has its challenges and threats. We are convinced that globalization, information technology, artificial intelligence and real-time communication are tools that help the integration and development of our peoples — of course, if they are used well. In that respect, there is a growing sense of responsibility among world leaders. I heard the Secretary-General emphasize that issue earlier today. We are in a world where speeches are actions; where, standing here, a world leader can generate consequences — be it an international conflict, a bank run or something else — just with his words.

In that forward-looking spirit, my country seeks to explore the potential opportunities provided by advanced technologies and to harness emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence, as essential tools to find innovative solutions for our businesses, lives and Government services. We believe that international attention and investments should be directed towards those technologies in order to accelerate sustainable development and achieve transformative shifts in addressing the challenges we face in different fields. That will allow us to bridge development gaps and support progress for all.

Access to information in a universal, equitable and financially affordable manner, as well as to the instruments providing access to it, is also one of the major challenges of modern times. The Internet claims to represent a relationship of rapprochement between spaces and peoples, but the so-called spider web favours rich countries while developing countries are still poorly connected, particularly in Africa. At a time when the world and trade are becoming increasingly digital, it is becoming imperative for all countries to have access to the Internet, including artificial intelligence, which is revolutionizing the world as we speak. The increasingly widening and gaping abyss between the countries of the global North and the global South is causing the latter to lose a large number of social, scientific and economic opportunities. As leaving no one behind is one of the pillars of United Nations action, it is more than urgent that the digital divide be bridged in the legitimate interest of current and future generations.
Secondly, Africa looks forward to addressing economic development and joining the revolutions currently taking place in the fields of artificial intelligence, digitalization and renewable energy.

Fifthly, the welcome role that the United Nations is trying to play in confronting emerging challenges, such as digital cooperation, crime, cybersecurity and artificial intelligence, should not make us forget the challenges related to the failure of the collective security system in the light of the inability of the United Nations system to implement its primary mission and even the justification for its establishment, the maintenance of international peace and security.

Technological innovations, artificial intelligence and social media are increasingly being used for incitement, terrorist recruitment and spreading hate speech, misinformation and disinformation, with adverse effects on cybersecurity. We must give due attention to that issue. Many young people have fallen victim to those negative practices. All of this proves that confronting that scourge requires international cooperation.

Transforming the international financial architecture is also imperative if we are to realize just and inclusive growth worldwide. We must therefore deliver on the Addis Ababa Action Agenda. We must lose no time in implementing the Global Digital Compact (resolution 79/1, annex I). The governance of new spheres of human activity, including artificial intelligence, the Internet and outer space, must keep up with the speed and scale at which those technologies are developing. New rules should place human dignity as the priority.

We live in a turbulent, volatile world that is going through unprecedented and extremely difficult times with tremendous challenges. Those challenges include armed conflicts, tensions in every corner of the globe, crises in multilateral institutions and the international system, a siege on the values of democracy by the twin threats of populism and authoritarianism, risks of cyberwarfare and the inappropriate application of artificial intelligence, the brutal inequity in the distribution of wealth, and climate change, which is endangering our very existence. Those are just some of the immense problems we are facing. I am afraid that I have not come here today to make a speech that will make us feel good, but rather one that will elicit the discomfort and concern that we should be feeling in the face of what is happening. I think that we must be honest and admit that we are failing — all of us — in building a better world. However, if there is a time and a place to debate and propose the crucial decisions that can change the course of humankind, it is the General Assembly. And thanks to the delicate situation we are living in, it is our duty to do so.

It is not late to breathe new life into the United Nations, but that can be achieved through the restoration of trust based on the Charter principle of the sovereign equality of all States, rather than through out-of-touch summits and declarations. However, trust is instead being undermined, including by actions of the West — in circumvention of the United Nations — to create subordinate, narrow formats to resolve crucial issues, such as control over the Internet or determination of legal frameworks to use artificial intelligence technologies. Those issues touch upon the future of all humankind and must be considered on a universal basis, without discrimination or aspirations to achieve unilateral benefits. Thus, everything has to be agreed on a fair basis involving all United Nations Members, and not how the socalled Pact for the Future (resolution 79/1) was drafted, without a single plenary round of talks attended by all countries. Instead, the work was done under the control of Western manipulators. As a result, the Pact merely swelled the ranks of declarations written in beautiful English before it was even born. Such, regrettably, is the fate of the outcomes of global summits of this kind.

The fourth International Conference on Small Island Developing States (SIDS4), held earlier this year, marked a significant milestone for all SIDS. We welcome the adoption of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS, which outlines an action plan for the next decade. Singapore will support our friends in SIDS. We launched a new technical assistance package at SIDS4, called SIDS of Change, which covers priority areas, including blue carbon. Singapore will continue to support our fellow small States, and we will share our development experience. I am happy to announce that Singapore will renew our capacity-building programme for the Forum of Small States (FOSS). We have labelled that programme FOSS for Good, a package that will offer digital-themed programmes, including Leadership and Governance in the Age of Digital Technologies and Artificial Intelligence.

We need a chart of United Nations as a common compass. Of course, we must adjust United Nations, but we must never forget the lesson of the League of Nations. When one forgets the principles When one abandons the principles on account of realpolitik, I mean the power or the powers of the moment, one forgets that no power is eternal, no personality is eternal. Empires went up and went down. We know by experience it. Colonial empires inside Europe, all kind of empires. went up and went down. We believe that in the reform of United Nations, we have three pillars, prevention, partnership, and protection. Preemptive action before the conflict, not just afterwards, mediation, preventive diplomacy. intervention of the Secretary General and of the PBC, avoiding distraction and institution collapse, building peace, fighting against the deep causes of violence, promoting resilient and peaceful societies. But development, peace building without development Preventive action without development does work. We co-presided together with an African partner, Burundi, the preparation of the Fourth Conference on Financing of Development. Ideas, dialogue, determination, results. Without sustainable development, no lasting peace is possible. Never forget to implement the 2030 agenda and the reform of the international financial architecture. It's a priority involving the digital, the space, the artificial intelligence technologies as force for peace, not tools for domination. Bridging the digital and technological divides is central to build resilient societies.

We reiterate the fact that we are available to accompany our brotherly countries in their work to achieve return to peace and stability. Through our history, we know that peace is difficult to build, but it is the only victory that benefits one and all. Ladies and gentlemen, your excellencies. guided by the same sense of responsibility. The recurring Ebola outbreaks and repeated pandemics have shown that global threats are no longer solely military or economic. Health security has become an essential component of collective security. And here, we will continue supporting the strengthening of the World Health Organization Regional Office for Africa in Brazzaville and will shoulder all of its responsibilities in accordance with the 1952 Headquarters Agreement. We also call for international governance of artificial intelligence in outer space. These technologies must remain in the service of humanity, progress, and the empowerment of peoples. Technological progress must not become a new instrument of domination. Africa must also be a center of creativity, innovation, and digital sovereignty. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, to conclude, the Republic of the Congo remains faithful to its principles, peace, development, sovereignty, good neighborliness, dialogue, cooperation, and mutual respect amongst nations. We will continue to defend our national interests while fulfilling our international responsibilities. We will continue to believe in Africa and in our shared destiny, and we will continue to choose the United Nations as a privileged space for dialogue amongst people. I thank you.

all it takes is one more step to push us over. Therefore, it is imperative to strengthen stability, security, and predictability. These are crucial elements of the enabling environment for peace. If any of them are undermined, peace will inevitably be weakened. After eight decades of the UN, This should have become our second nature. Instead, what we are actually seeing is a weaponization of everything. A mindset of extreme competition has set in, undermining institutions and establishing choke points. It extends from the world of finance to constricting market access, disrupting supply chains, and withholding technology. Resources and connectivity have become particularly subject to leveraging. As a result, nations are now more focused on de-risking and diversifying. Now, while this may secure their interest to varying degrees, the overall atmosphere is no longer that of trust or goodwill. Mr. President, the predicament of the global South is particularly acute. It faces a 4F crisis of the security of food, fuel, fertilizer, and finance. The combined impact of a super El Nino, compounding fertilizer shortages, and now impediments to grain movements, all these are cause for alarm. Moreover, SDG progress is under increasing pressure. The global South's right to industrialize is also undermined by non-market practices and market denial. The march of technology that was meant to instill hope has now become a source of anxiety. Misuse of AI is sharpening bias and diluting mutual respect. These directions bode ill for the aims and objectives of the United Nations. A persistent threat to peace has been the scourge of terrorism. That this could be state-sponsored with cross-border purpose makes it a direct affront to the global order. Governments indulging in such practices must be held accountable. There must be no dilution in our zero-tolerance approach towards terrorism. Its financial aspects, in particular, should be exposed and should be countered. Mr. President, yesterday, a serial practitioner of terrorism misrepresented facts before this Assembly. Arguments were invoked to normalise terrorism and claim immunity from its consequences. That will not stand. Our right to defend ourselves against terrorism will be exercised. Mr.

President, This week has also seen an intense debate on harnessing the potential of artificial intelligence. But perhaps what we are discovering in these conversations are our own limits to understanding what that potential might be. Reporting from the most powerful and well-capitalized AI companies tell us that we are on a precipice either of a technology-fueled utopia or an apocalypse. Whether we achieve one or the other, unfortunately, has been treated as a secondary priority to the AI race, one that has no clear finish line and, for that matter, a dubious prize. Liechtenstein supports the regulation of artificial intelligence. Unless we have a clear understanding of the methods, processes and purposes of the huge variety of AI systems, how can we risk the consequences to human rights, to our environment, to the long term capacities for our critical thinking and ultimately to the future of the human species? We are already seeing the impacts on civilians as armed forces increasingly integrate AI capabilities into their targeting systems in warfare. AI tools have to be made for humanity, lest we become the source material for AI systems to use, or merely the victims in its crosshairs. President, many of us standing here this week have mused about the UN's imperfections or expressed our concerns about its diminished relevance. The UN is indeed in a fragile place, but very few of us want to live in a world in which the United Nations is rendered obsolete. On the contrary, we realize how much we need the UN. In the often repeated quote, the UN was not built to take us to heaven, but in an era where it might not even be able to save us from hell, this Universal Organization retains the unparalleled ability to meet us where we are. It is up to us to do what we can to bring it closer to carrying out its mission under the UN Charter. Liechtenstein commits to doing our part with you all in service of multilateralism and of the peoples we serve. Thank you.

A handful of private actors now control how billions of people communicate, work, transact, and consume information. Artificial intelligence is changing how economies cooperate, how societies function, and how governments make decisions. The opportunities are enormous. but also are the risks. We must therefore ask simple question, who governs the transformation? Technology must serve humanity, never the reverse. And the answer cannot be that small number of companies or countries decide the rules for everyone else. The United Nations must continue to empower global south countries who are likely to be more greatly affected by an equitable AI development to participate in global discussion on AI. The global South cannot simply become a destination for data centers while decisions about AI are made elsewhere. We must be partners in innovation, not merely customers and market, and not merely destinations for investment. Partners involved in the decisions that will shape our future. Equitable decision making and equitable development. That means managing the enormous demands that tech infrastructure places on water, energy, land, and other resources so that the benefits of AI can be shared more broadly across the borders. Mr. President, in our hyper-connected world today, indeed, very few things stay where they begin. Technologies are rapidly shared, and they can just as rapidly disrupt. Similarly, war can also travel beyond borders. Across West Asia, escalating conflict threatens some of the world's most important routes for energy and trade, including the Strait of Hormuz, and the Bab al-Mandab. The consequences of conflict do not stop at these shores. A family in Southeast Asia has no part in these disputes, yet that family still pays the price when food, fuel, and cost of living rise. Malaysia therefore urges all parties to step back from escalation. Diplomacy has shown that dialogue is possible, that past must not be abandoned. Or we risk sending further shockwaves through global markets and needlessly bringing suffering to innocent families around the world. Mr. President, most nations in this hall are not great powers, yet Decision taken by few can shape the future for all.

While the pact gives due consideration for the interest and the needs of the future generation, its implementation has not been as effective as we had wished. For Namibia, effective implementation of the key commitment of the Pact for the Future would be beneficial in accomplishing Namibia's national priorities, namely agriculture, sports, youth empowerment, quality education and training, creative industry, health and social welfare, land, housing, and sanitation. I wish to urge all member states to consider the implementation of the Pact for the Future as a crucial international priority for development. As part of our developmental agenda, we are preparing our young people for the emerging industries in Namibia, such as oil and gas, renewable energy, and green hydrogen, among others. Subsequently, this year we have introduced 100% subsidised registration and tuition fees for Namibian students entering universities and vocational training centres and encourage them to take up appropriate courses. The Government of Namibia has established the National Youth Development Fund last year. As a result of this fund, young people have set up their own medical practice, law firms milling plants, pottery business, to mention a few, thus contributing to job creation and poverty eradication. Namibia also takes cognizance of the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence in advancing human progress in line with the Global Digital Compact. However, We call for ethical, responsible, inclusive, and human-centered development and use of artificial intelligence with appropriate safeguard to ensure that technological advancement complements and enhance human capability rather than undermine it. A United Nations that delivers for all must be inclusive. I reaffirm Namibia's unwavering solidarity with the people denied their right to self-determination. This position is firmly rooted in Namibia's historical experience of the brutality and colonialism apartheid and occupation.

Our commitment to peace is summed up in the words of a distinguished Paraguayan, Manuel Gondra. Since we cannot ensure that the just are always strong, we must strive to ensure that the strong are always just. Paraguay wishes to shoulder greater responsibilities within the system, but this system as it stands simply isn't working. That is why we believe that the selection of the next Secretary-General will be a fundamental decision. The time has come for that leadership to come from Latin America and the Caribbean. Our region has a vocation for peace, dialogue and multilateralism, and it has candidates that are capable of taking up that responsibility. We need a Secretary-General who restores the organization's political leadership, one that strengthens preventive diplomacy, acts before crises become irreversible, and one that listens to the states and the peoples whom this organization serves. In short, the Security Council must cease to be a pretty snapshot of the world as it was in 1945. It must listen more closely to this assembly and must not remain paralyzed when peace is threatened. We need a UN for 2026 or for 2050, not one for 1945. Only then will the United Nations be able to truly deliver for all of its members. This Assembly also calls on us to manage transformation. No one here needs me to tell them what the great transformation of our age is. Every great era in human history has had its driving force. Steam powered the industrial revolution. The transistor powered the digital age. No force in our time is as profound as artificial intelligence. We can already see its power in warfare, in the economy, and in our everyday lives. Unlike tools that merely transmitted what we said, these systems are part and parcel of the decisions that we make. The potential is immense. Paraguay today feeds 100 million people, and with this tool, it could feed 1 billion. It could enable us to cover in years distances that once took generations. This transformation cannot be held back and no one should be left out of it.

Global action on disaster resilience and predictable financing for a just energy transition is essential if international cooperation is to deliver for all. Our continent has the world's largest reserves of critical minerals. These critical minerals can help bridge the gap between wealth and poor nations and overcome the indignities of poverty and underdevelopment. We insist, Mr. President, that indeed, Africa must have a stake in shaping the rules that govern the development and the deployment of artificial intelligence. We have a youthful population ready to play a key role in the beneficiation at source of critical minerals and research and innovations for artificial intelligence. Restoring trust in multilateralism demands that we demonstrate, as the United Nations, that peaceful resolutions of conflicts is still our mantra. Unfortunately, much of what we see runs counter to this. In the last two years, the world spent more on military budgets than on resourcing this important body tasked with maintaining global peace. We are reminded that meeting the SDGs by 2030, including ending hunger and expanding access to safe water and sanitation, will require not more than 5% of the 2.9 trillion US dollars spent on arms. The results of the choice we are making is an arms race and the world as divided as it is dangerous. We see the consequences in Sudan, which is today the worst humanitarian crisis in the world. We see also the consequences in the Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, in Iran, Ukraine, and elsewhere, humanitarian workers are caught in the crossfires of today's conflict. When they are not being obstructed from reaching civilians in need, they are being killed in the line of duty. To restore respect for international law, we must protect those who deliver humanitarian assistance. That is why South Africa endorses the Declaration for the Protection of Humanitarian Personnel, supported by nearly 120 states, from all regions of the world. Mr. President, 80 years ago, the first resolution of the General Assembly called for the elimination of nuclear weapons.
